name: povray
why: Old-school ray tracer where you write a scene description and watch light geometry become images.

brief.what_it_is: POV-Ray (Persistence Of Vision RAYtracer) is a free, open-source ray tracer for making three-dimensional graphics. The homepage calls it 'a high-quality, Free Software tool for creating stunning three-dimensional graphics.' The scout notes describe it as an old-school ray tracer where you write a scene description and watch geometry become images. I did not find the scene-file syntax on the pages I read, so the input format is unverified beyond that description. The output is a rendered image. The source code is published for anyone who wants to do their own ports.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage gives no problem statement of its own. Its news ties the project to DKBTrace, a raytracer by David K. Buck, whose source code became the foundation of POV-Ray; the site says POV-Ray 'would not exist if it were not for David's kind contribution of the DKBTrace source code.' The first beta is dated July 29, 1991.
brief.install_notes: Homepage links to a separate download page, which I did not fetch, so I have no platform-by-platform install steps. Windows is the sore spot: the November 2024 development note says official Windows releases are supposed to be code-signed, but the project has no valid signing key because its old one expired, and it has been unable to get a new one verified. The site says it is a policy that official Windows releases must be signed. The brew formula is named povray and installs an executable named povray, per the metadata given.
brief.standout: It is a long-lived, free ray tracer with a documented lineage back to DKBTrace and a first beta in 1991. The homepage's news is unusually candid about its own problems, including a 2021 hardware failure, a 2026 transit outage, and a stalled Windows code-signing effort.
brief.status: quiet. The November 2024 development note says development is resuming after a long break in 3.8 beta releases, 'though not at the pace of past releases.' The newest news items are from March 2026 (an outage that the site says was resolved), December 2025 (an unrelated Kickstarter by the DKBTrace author), and February 2022 (3.8 beta availability). The documentation page lists 3.7 as current and 3.6 as older. I did not check a release date or commit log.
brief.caveats: I did not read a README: the homepage is not a GitHub repository, so the tool returned the site HTML, not a README. I saw no command lines anywhere in the pages I fetched. The documentation index is only a version selector, and I did not open the 3.7 docs themselves. The Windows release signing problem is unresolved as of the November 2024 note. The site has had several outages (a 2021 hardware failure and a 2026 transit black-holing that the site says is now resolved). The homepage news says 3.8 is still in beta. I did not check the license text, so I can only say 'Free Software' per the homepage.

judge.reason: POV-Ray’s scene-description language turns geometry, materials, and light into rendered images—a distinctive, hands-on way to explore ray tracing beyond ordinary 3D tools.

entry.title: POV-Ray
entry.tldr: A ray tracer from 1991 where you write a text description of a scene and the program renders it as a three-dimensional image.
entry.deeper_look:
POV-Ray, the Persistence Of Vision RAYtracer, is a free ray tracer for making three-dimensional graphics. You describe a scene in a text file, and the program works out how light would travel through it and writes out an image. The homepage calls it "a high-quality, Free Software tool for creating stunning three-dimensional graphics." The brief did not cover the scene-file syntax, so look at the documentation for the details.

Its lineage is documented. The site says POV-Ray "would not exist if it were not for David's kind contribution of the DKBTrace source code," a raytracer by David K. Buck. The first beta is dated July 29, 1991, which makes this one of the older graphics tools still around.

The idea underneath is that an image can be a program's output rather than something you draw. You write down geometry, materials and lights, and the renderer does the rest. That is a way into ray tracing, procedural scenes and how rendering works. The source is published, and the site notes it is "available for those wanting to do their own ports."

entry.whats_unique: It is a long-lived free ray tracer with a documented lineage back to DKBTrace and a first beta in 1991. You build images by writing a scene description rather than using a modelling GUI.
entry.caveats: Development is quiet: 3.8 is still in beta after a long break, the docs list 3.7 as current, and the project says official Windows releases are stuck on an expired code-signing key.
